lessons.title: Common, Proper and Collective Nouns
lessons.content:
# Nouns & Classifications

## Names and what they name

A noun names a person, place, object, material, group, or idea. *Teacher*, *market*, and *river* are **common nouns**: each names a general kind of thing. A **proper noun** identifies one particular person or place, such as *Amina*, *Kano*, or *River Niger*. Proper nouns begin with capital letters. The word *river* stays common in *the river*; in *River Niger*, it is part of the name.

A **collective noun** treats several members as a group: *a class of pupils*, *a flock of birds*, *a committee of parents*. The group word is the noun; *of pupils* tells us who belongs to it.

## Read the sentence, not just the word

In “Amina left her book at the market,” *Amina* is proper, while *book* and *market* are common. In “The choir rehearsed,” *choir* names a collection of singers. Capitalisation helps, but sentence position can also capitalize a word: *The* at the start of a sentence is not a proper noun.

## A closer look at names

Names of particular people, towns, rivers, schools, and organisations are proper nouns: *Musa*, *Enugu*, *River Benue*, and *Unity Secondary School*. Days and months are also proper nouns, as in *Monday* and *October*. A person's job is not proper by itself: write *the doctor*, but capitalise the title when it forms part of a name, as in *Doctor Okafor*. Titles such as *Mr* and *Mrs* follow the same distinction.

Read this example: “The pupils visited the museum beside the River Benue.” *Pupils* and *museum* name general kinds of people and places, so they are common nouns. *River Benue* identifies one river and is proper. If a sentence begins with *The*, its capital letter comes from its position, not from the word being a name. When classifying nouns, ask what a word identifies and use the sentence to decide whether it names a particular individual or a general kind.

assessmentSeed.prompt: Which noun names a particular place and therefore takes a capital letter?

lessons.title: Countable, Uncountable and Abstract Nouns
lessons.content:
# Nouns & Classifications

## Counting nouns and measuring amounts

A **countable noun** can be counted as separate items and normally has singular and plural forms: *one exercise book, four exercise books*. A singular countable noun usually needs a determiner: *a pencil*, *the pencil*. An **uncountable noun** is treated as a mass or whole rather than as separate units: *water, rice, advice,* and *information*. To count it, supply a unit: *two cups of water*, *three bags of rice*, *a piece of advice*.

An **abstract noun** names an idea, quality, feeling, or state, such as *honesty*, *fear*, or *childhood*. Abstract does not automatically mean uncountable. We can speak of *an experience* or *several ideas* when we mean distinct examples.

## Let the noun guide the quantity word

Use *many* with countable plurals (*many questions*) and *much* with uncountable nouns (*much information*). *Some* and *a lot of* can work with either. In standard usage, *information* and *advice* do not take a plural *-s*: write *two pieces of advice*, not *two advices*.

## Choose a quantity that fits

Countability affects more than plural endings. Use *fewer* with items that can be counted (*fewer exercise books*) and *less* with an amount treated as a mass (*less water*). In conversation, *less* is sometimes used broadly, but the distinction makes formal writing precise. Use *how many* for countable nouns and *how much* for uncountable ones: *How many questions? How much time?*

Some nouns change meaning with countability. *Chicken* can mean meat as a mass or individual birds: *We ate chicken*; *The farmer raised six chickens*. Likewise, *paper* can mean material or a newspaper/document: *a sheet of paper*; *two papers to read*. These are not exceptions to memorise blindly; the meaning determines whether separate units are intended.

When editing a sentence, identify the noun first, then choose its determiner and verb form. “There is some information” treats the noun as a mass. “There are three pieces of information” counts the units, not the information itself.

assessmentSeed.prompt: Which phrase correctly counts an uncountable noun?

lessons.title: Plural Forms, Possession and Noun Use
lessons.content:
# Nouns & Classifications

## Plural endings are not all alike

Most nouns form the plural with *-s*: *desk/desks*. Add *-es* after many endings that already make a hissing sound: *class/classes*, *wish/wishes*, *box/boxes*. For a consonant followed by *y*, change *y* to *ies*: *city/cities*; after a vowel, keep the *y*: *key/keys*. Some forms must be learned individually: *child/children*, *foot/feet*.

## Apostrophes show possession

An apostrophe marks ownership or association, not plurality. *The pupil's bag* belongs to one pupil; *the pupils' bags* belong to several. The plural is made first, then the apostrophe is placed after its final *s*. Irregular plurals without a final *s* take *'s*: *the children's books*.

A noun may also modify another noun. In *school bus*, *school* tells us what kind of bus; it does not mean the bus owns a school. Compare *the school's bus*, which does express a relationship of possession. These small spelling choices change the meaning of the whole phrase.

## Edit the ending, then check the meaning

Plural spelling and possession answer different questions. In *the pupils' books*, the plural noun *pupils* tells us there is more than one pupil; the apostrophe after *s* shows that the books are associated with them. In *the pupil's books*, one pupil has several books. Read the phrase aloud if the punctuation is confusing, then ask how many owners it describes.

For a singular noun ending in *s*, many styles accept either *James's bag* or *James' bag*. Follow the style expected by your school and remain consistent. Do not use an apostrophe to form ordinary plurals: *three desks*, not *three desk's*. Plural nouns that do not end in *s* form possession with *'s*: *the children's playground*.

Try revising “The girls uniform was wet.” If one girl owns the uniform, write *the girl's uniform*. If several girls own uniforms, write *the girls' uniforms*. The apostrophe and the noun ending both carry information, so proofreading them is part of proofreading meaning.

assessmentSeed.prompt: Which phrase means that a book belongs to several pupils?

lessons.title: Matching Verbs to Singular and Plural Subjects
lessons.content:
# Subject-Verb Concord

## Make the verb agree with its subject

**Concord** is the grammatical agreement between a subject and its verb. In the simple present tense, a singular third-person subject usually takes a verb ending in *-s*: *The learner reads*. A plural subject takes the base form: *The learners read*. This is the reverse of the noun pattern, where *-s* often marks a plural.

Find the subject before choosing the verb. In “The basket of mangoes is on the table,” *basket* is the subject; *of mangoes* is a phrase describing it. The nearby plural noun does not control the verb. A useful check is to remove the phrase: “The basket is on the table.”

In the past tense, most verbs have the same form for singular and plural subjects: *She walked; they walked*. The verb *be* is an exception: *I was*, but *we were*.

Try the same method with “The teacher and the pupils ___ ready.” The joined subject names more than one person, so the correct form is *are*.

## Use the subject as your anchor

A subject can be a noun, a pronoun, or a longer phrase. In “The youngest player in the teams is our captain,” the complete subject is *the youngest player in the teams*; its main noun is singular *player*. The plural *teams* sits inside a phrase and does not determine the verb. Find the head noun—the central noun in the subject—before checking agreement.

Questions can change the usual order without changing agreement. In “Where are the books?” the subject *books* follows the verb, but it is still plural. In a command such as “Close the window,” the subject *you* is understood even though it is not written. In questions with *does*, the verb after the subject stays in its base form: “Does the learner read?” not “Does the learner reads?” The auxiliary already carries the third-person ending.

These checks are useful when a sentence has extra phrases or unusual word order. Agreement follows the grammatical subject, not the nearest noun or the apparent meaning of one nearby word.

assessmentSeed.prompt: Choose the verb that agrees with the subject: 'The basket of oranges ___ full.'

lessons.title: Compound Subjects and Words Between Subject and Verb
lessons.content:
# Subject-Verb Concord

## Subjects joined together

Two subjects joined by *and* usually name more than one person or thing and take a plural verb: *Bola and Musa walk to school*. Meaning can make a difference. When two nouns name one dish or a single combined idea, a singular verb is natural: *Rice and beans is today's lunch*.

With *either…or* and *neither…nor*, the verb generally agrees with the nearer subject: *Either the teacher or the pupils are leading*; *Either the pupils or the teacher is leading*. If the sentence sounds strained, put the plural subject nearer the verb or rewrite it.

## Do not let extra phrases take over

A phrase between the subject and verb does not usually change the subject's number: *The head teacher, together with the staff, is attending*. The subject is still *head teacher*.

Compare the full subject before deciding: in “The nurse and the driver are here,” two people are present; in “Bread and tea is my usual breakfast,” the speaker treats the meal as one combination. The verb reflects the meaning of the subject, not simply the closest noun.

## Keep coordinated subjects clear

When *and* joins two separate people or things, use a plural verb: “The chalk and the duster are on the table.” A phrase such as *as well as* does not work like *and*: “The class captain, as well as two prefects, is speaking.” The main subject is *captain*; the extra phrase adds information without making a compound subject.

With *either…or* and *neither…nor*, proximity agreement helps, but parallel wording is just as important. “Either the teacher or the pupils are presenting” is easier to read than a long sentence with many words between the alternatives and the verb. If the nearest-subject rule produces an awkward result, restructure the sentence: “The pupils or the teacher will present.”

Do not treat every pair as one unit. “The principal and the secretary are meeting” names two people; “Fish and yam is served today” may name one meal. The intended meaning determines whether the coordinated subject is one idea or two separate subjects.

assessmentSeed.prompt: Which verb agrees with the compound subject in 'Musa and Amina ___ the debate'?

lessons.title: Indefinite Subjects and Tricky Concord
lessons.content:
# Subject-Verb Concord

## Singular words with plural-looking neighbours

Words such as *each*, *everyone*, *everybody*, *someone*, and *neither* are grammatically singular: *Everyone has a notebook*. In “Each of the players is ready,” the subject is *each*, not *players*. The phrase after *of* identifies the people being discussed; it does not change the verb.

Amounts and titles are also often treated as one unit: *Ten kilometres is a long distance*; *Mathematics is on the timetable*. Some nouns that look singular refer to paired objects and take plural verbs: *The scissors are blunt*. In *a pair of scissors is on the desk*, the subject is *pair*.

## When the meaning determines the choice

*A number of pupils are waiting* means several pupils are waiting. *The number of pupils is increasing* treats the total as one figure. Both are correct because the grammatical subjects differ. With *none*, choose a verb that makes the intended sense clear; in careful writing, recast an awkward sentence rather than leave readers guessing.

## Watch phrases that describe a total

Some expressions look plural because they contain a plural noun, while their grammatical subject is singular. In “Every one of the players has a number,” the head of the subject is *one*, so use *has*. Compare this with “All the players have numbers,” where *players* is the subject. Words such as *each*, *either*, and *neither* also take singular verbs in standard school English.

Measurements usually take a singular verb when they describe one total: “Five litres is enough for the experiment.” When the sentence refers to separate items, the noun may be plural: “Five litres of water were poured into separate bottles” can emphasise the individual portions. Meaning and sentence construction work together.

For a difficult sentence, first cross out descriptive phrases mentally, then identify the head of the subject. Check whether it names one unit, several individuals, or a pair of objects. Finally, read the sentence aloud; a mismatch often becomes clearer when the subject and verb are heard together.

assessmentSeed.prompt: Choose the correct verb: 'Each of the players ___ a number.'

lessons.title: Adjectives: Description, Quantity and Comparison
lessons.content:
# Adjectives & Adverbs

## Adjectives give nouns detail

An adjective describes or limits a noun or pronoun: *a careful driver*, *three ripe mangoes*, *their classroom*. It may appear before the noun or after a linking verb: *The road is narrow*; *The soup smells spicy*. In the second sentence, *spicy* describes the soup; it does not tell how the soup smells.

Adjectives also compare. For many short adjectives, add *-er* for two things and *-est* for a group: *tall, taller, tallest*. Longer adjectives often use *more* and *most*: *more careful*, *most interesting*. Some forms are irregular: *good, better, best*. Avoid doubling the comparison: *more taller* is not standard.

## Compare like with like

Use a comparative with *than*: *This path is shorter than that one*. A superlative identifies the extreme within a group: *This is the shortest of the three paths*. The items being compared should belong to the same category, so the reader can tell exactly what is being judged.

## Choose a comparison form carefully

Spelling can change when a comparative ending is added. A short adjective ending in consonant plus *y* often changes *y* to *i*: *happy, happier, happiest*. Some short adjectives double their final consonant: *big, bigger, biggest*. Longer adjectives usually take *more* and *most*, though common usage varies. When unsure, consult a dictionary rather than combining both patterns.

Comparisons should state the group being compared. “Amina is the taller of the two sisters” uses a comparative because there are two. “Amina is the tallest in her class” uses a superlative because she is being compared with a group. Avoid saying *the most tallest*, which applies two superlative forms at once.

Adjectives also make descriptions more exact without comparison. In “three narrow paths,” *three* tells quantity and *narrow* describes width. In “the path seems narrow,” the adjective follows a linking verb and still describes the path. Identifying the noun an adjective belongs to is more reliable than relying on its position alone.

assessmentSeed.prompt: Which is the correct comparative form of 'careful'?

lessons.title: Adverbs: How, When, Where and How Often
lessons.content:
# Adjectives & Adverbs

## Words that modify actions and descriptions

An adverb modifies a verb, an adjective, or another adverb. It can tell how, when, where, or how often: *She spoke quietly*; *We arrived yesterday*; *The children waited outside*; *He often practises*. Many manner adverbs end in *-ly*, but the ending is not a reliable test by itself. *Fast* and *hard* can be adverbs; *hardly* means “almost not,” as in *I could hardly hear the bell*.

In *a very clear answer*, *very* modifies the adjective *clear*. In *They moved quite slowly*, *quite* modifies the adverb *slowly*. Compare *a careful reader* with *the reader works carefully*: *careful* describes a person, while *carefully* tells how the person works.

Some common comparisons are irregular: *well, better, best* and *badly, worse, worst*. Choose the form by its role in the sentence, not by adding *-ly* mechanically.

## Adverbs can change the force of a sentence

An adverb is not always a word ending in *-ly*. In “The bus arrived late,” *late* tells when; in “The bus is late,” it describes the bus after the linking verb and is an adjective. Words such as *daily* may be adjectives or adverbs depending on their use: *a daily lesson*; *They practise daily*. Sentence role matters more than spelling.

Frequency adverbs include *always*, *usually*, *often*, *sometimes*, and *never*. They tend to come before an ordinary main verb (*We usually walk*) but after an auxiliary (*We have often walked*) and after *be* (*We are usually early*). These positions make the sentence easy to follow, though writers may move an adverb for emphasis.

Compare “She nearly walked five kilometres” with “She walked nearly five kilometres.” In the first, *nearly* suggests she almost walked but may not have; in the second, she walked a distance close to five kilometres. The adverb's placement identifies what the speaker means.

assessmentSeed.prompt: Which word is the adverb of manner in 'The class listened carefully'?

lessons.title: Adjective and Adverb Placement in Sentences
lessons.content:
# Adjectives & Adverbs

## Placement shapes meaning

Put an adjective near the noun it describes: *The careful driver checked the tyre*. Manner adverbs often follow a verb or its object: *She answered politely*. Frequency adverbs usually precede a main verb (*She often reads*) but follow a form of *be* (*She is often early*). Their position can vary for emphasis, but a reader should not have to guess what they modify.

The word *only* is especially sensitive to placement. *Only Kemi borrowed the atlas* means no one else borrowed it. *Kemi borrowed only the atlas* means she borrowed nothing else. Moving the word changes the focus of the sentence.

## Repair the dangling description

An opening modifier should describe the subject that follows it. “Walking to school, the rain soaked Tunde” accidentally makes the rain the walker. Rewrite it as “As Tunde walked to school, the rain soaked him.” A quick proofread should ask: who is performing the action in the opening phrase, and is that person or thing named next?

## Put the limiting word beside its target

The position of a modifier can alter not only emphasis but the facts a sentence communicates. “I nearly read every page” means I came close to reading all of them; “I read nearly every page” means I read most of them. When revising, move *only*, *nearly*, or *almost* beside the word or phrase it limits, then check that the revised meaning matches your intention.

A modifier can also be misplaced when a sentence begins with an introductory phrase. “After finishing the assignment, the television was switched on” makes it sound as if the television finished the work. Name the person who did it: “After finishing the assignment, Chika switched on the television.”

Not every long sentence is unclear, but modifiers should have an obvious target. During proofreading, underline each descriptive phrase and draw a mental line to the noun or action it describes. If two targets seem possible, rewrite the sentence rather than expecting the reader to infer the intended one.

assessmentSeed.prompt: Where does the frequency adverb usually go in 'She ___ visits the library'?

lessons.title: Recognising Transitive and Intransitive Verbs
lessons.content:
# Transitive Verbs

## Does the verb have an object?

A transitive verb has a direct object: the person or thing affected by the action. In “The baker kneaded the dough,” *dough* answers *kneaded what?* and is the object. An intransitive verb has no direct object: in “The baby slept peacefully,” nothing receives the action of *slept*.

Many verbs can be used either way. The bell *rang* has no object; the caretaker *rang the bell* does. It is the verb's use in the sentence—not the verb alone—that determines whether it is transitive.

A noun after a verb is not always its direct object. In “The pupils laughed at the joke,” *joke* is the object of the preposition *at*. By contrast, in “The pupils opened the windows,” *windows* is directly connected to *opened*.

To analyse a sentence, find the verb, then ask what or whom the action affects. If no answer fits without adding a preposition, the verb may be intransitive in that sentence.

## Some verbs change their pattern

The same verb may be transitive in one sentence and intransitive in another. “The pupils grow maize” has a direct object, *maize*, so *grow* is transitive. “The pupils grow quickly” has no direct object; *quickly* describes how they grow, so the verb is intransitive here. The question *what?* is a useful first test, but make sure the answer is not simply a time, place, or manner phrase.

A linking verb works differently from both patterns: it connects the subject to a description or identity. In “The soup tastes salty,” *salty* describes *soup*; it is not an object receiving an action. Compare “The cook tasted the soup,” where *soup* is the direct object of the action *tasted*.

When analysing a sentence, locate the main verb and ask what relationship follows it. Is something affected by an action, is there no object, or does the verb link the subject to a description? This prevents every noun after a verb from being labelled an object.

assessmentSeed.prompt: Which sentence uses 'opened' transitively?

lessons.title: Direct Objects and Indirect Objects
lessons.content:
# Transitive Verbs

## Objects and recipients

A **direct object** names what a transitive verb acts on. An **indirect object** names the recipient or beneficiary. In “The teacher gave the class an assignment,” the teacher gave *an assignment* (direct object) to *the class* (indirect object). Both objects belong to the same verb, but they answer different questions.

The recipient can also be introduced by a preposition: “The teacher gave an assignment to the class.” Here *assignment* remains the direct object; *class* is the object of *to*, not an indirect object in the sentence's grammatical form. A verb can also have only a direct object: “The teacher gave an assignment.”

## Trace each relationship

Ask *gave what?* to find *assignment*, then *gave it to whom?* to find *class*. In “The librarian sent her colleague a timetable,” *timetable* is the thing sent and *colleague* is the recipient. Rewriting the sentence with *to* makes the two roles easier to see: “The librarian sent a timetable to her colleague.”

## Two objects, two roles

Verbs such as *give*, *send*, *show*, and *offer* often take both a thing and a recipient. In “Musa sent his sister a message,” the message is the direct object: it is what Musa sent. His sister is the indirect object: she is the person who received it. A useful rewording is “Musa sent a message to his sister.”

The indirect object usually appears before the direct object without a preposition. When *to* or *for* introduces the recipient, that noun phrase is the object of the preposition instead. Compare “The coach bought the team new shirts” with “The coach bought new shirts for the team.” In both sentences, *shirts* are what was bought, but the grammatical construction differs.

Some verbs cannot use both patterns naturally. We say “explain the rule to the class,” not usually “explain the class the rule.” Learn the pattern with the verb rather than assuming every recipient can move before the direct object.

assessmentSeed.prompt: In 'Musa sent his sister a message', what is the direct object?

lessons.title: Objects, Passive Voice and Object Complements
lessons.content:
# Transitive Verbs

## Passive voice shifts the focus

In an active sentence, the subject performs the action: “The pupils cleaned the room.” In the passive, the object becomes the subject: “The room was cleaned by the pupils.” The passive form uses *be* plus a past participle (*was cleaned*). It is useful when the result matters more than the doer, or when the doer is unknown: “The window was broken overnight.” A *by*-phrase can be included when the actor matters.

## Complements describe the object

An **object complement** renames or describes the direct object. In “The class elected Amina captain,” *Amina* is the object and *captain* gives her new role. In “The news made him anxious,” *him* is the object and *anxious* describes his state. Neither *captain* nor *anxious* receives a second action; each adds information about the object.

To distinguish an object complement from another object, ask whether the final word names a separate thing affected by the verb or tells us what the first object became or was like.

## Form the passive without losing the tense

To change an active sentence to passive, move its direct object into subject position and use the appropriate form of *be* with the past participle. “The workers repair the bridge” becomes “The bridge is repaired by the workers.” For a past action, “The workers repaired the bridge” becomes “The bridge was repaired by the workers.” The tense is carried by *is* or *was*; *repaired* stays a past participle.

The passive is not automatically better or more formal. It is useful when the receiver or result is the topic, or when the actor is unknown: “The missing file was found.” If the actor matters, keep the *by*-phrase; if it does not, omit it. Too many passive sentences can hide who is responsible for an action.

An object complement stays connected to the object rather than becoming a second object. In “They painted the door red,” *door* receives the action and *red* describes the result. The adjective does not name another thing that was painted.

assessmentSeed.prompt: Which word is the object complement in 'The class elected Amina captain'?

lessons.title: IPv4 Addresses and Network Prefixes
lessons.content:
# IPv4 Subnetting

## An address is a 32-bit number

An IPv4 address contains 32 binary digits, grouped into four octets. Dotted decimal notation makes those groups easier to read: 192.168.10.25. Each octet represents eight bits and ranges from 0 to 255. A subnet prefix marks how many leading bits identify the network. In 192.168.10.0/24, 24 bits identify the network and the remaining eight identify addresses within it.

The prefix can also be written as a subnet mask. A /24 is 255.255.255.0: the first three octets are network bits. A /26 is 255.255.255.192; its final octet uses two network bits and leaves six host bits.

## Why a boundary matters

The prefix is what allows a device or router to decide whether another address is local or must be reached through a router. A /24 contains 256 total addresses; in an ordinary subnet, the network and broadcast addresses are reserved, leaving 254 host addresses. The same address with a different prefix can belong to a different network.

## See the boundary in binary

Each bit in an octet has a place value: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, or 1. The decimal value 192 is 128 + 64, so its binary form is 11000000. That is why the final octet of a /26 mask, 255.255.255.192, begins with two network bits followed by six host bits. The prefix counts the network bits from the beginning of the 32-bit address.

For example, /24 uses 24 network bits and leaves one complete 8-bit octet for hosts. A /25 uses one additional network bit from that octet and leaves seven host bits. The dotted mask for /25 is 255.255.255.128. The visual pattern in a mask must be contiguous: network bits come first, then host bits.

Subnetting is a way to divide address space according to network needs. A small office segment may need fewer host addresses than a large school network. Choosing a prefix is therefore both a calculation and a planning decision.

assessmentSeed.prompt: How many bits are in an IPv4 address?

lessons.title: Calculating Subnet Size and Host Range
lessons.content:
# IPv4 Subnetting

## Calculate the block before listing hosts

For a prefix /n, the number of host bits is 32 minus n. A /26 leaves six host bits, so the block contains 2^6 = 64 addresses. In a conventional subnet, one address identifies the network and one is the broadcast address; 62 remain for hosts.

Consider 192.168.10.0/26. Its mask is 255.255.255.192. The final octet advances in blocks of 64, giving subnet boundaries at 0, 64, 128, and 192. In the first block, .0 is the network address, .1 through .62 are host addresses, and .63 is the broadcast address. The next block begins at .64.

## Check the arithmetic

Where a mask octet is partial, subtract it from 256 to find the block size: 256 - 192 = 64. For a /27, five host bits give 32 addresses; the mask ends in 224, and 256 - 224 also gives 32. This cross-check catches many off-by-one errors.

## Compare two common subnet sizes

A /25 leaves seven host bits, so it contains 2^7 = 128 total addresses. Under the conventional IPv4 rule, subtract the network and broadcast addresses to get 126 usable host addresses. Its mask is 255.255.255.128, so blocks in the last octet begin at 0 and 128.

A /28 leaves four host bits: 2^4 = 16 total addresses, or 14 conventional host addresses. Its mask ends in 240 because 240 is 128 + 64 + 32 + 16. The block size is 256 - 240 = 16, so boundaries occur at 0, 16, 32, 48, and so on. These examples show that a longer prefix leaves fewer host bits and creates smaller subnets.

The subtraction of two applies to ordinary subnets, where the network and broadcast addresses have their traditional roles. Special-purpose prefixes can follow different rules, so use the convention required by the problem. Always state whether you are counting total addresses or usable host addresses.

assessmentSeed.prompt: How many usable host addresses are in a conventional IPv4 /26 subnet?

lessons.title: Finding a Network, Broadcast and Host Address
lessons.content:
# IPv4 Subnetting

## Locate the address inside its block

Find the network, broadcast, and host range for 192.168.10.77/26. A /26 advances by 64 in the final octet: 0, 64, 128, 192. Since 77 lies between 64 and 127, the network address is 192.168.10.64 and the broadcast address is 192.168.10.127. The conventional usable host range is .65 through .126.

The address itself is not necessarily the network address. Nor does every subnet end in .0; the prefix determines the boundaries. A /24 containing this address has different boundaries from its /26 subdivisions.

## A repeatable method

Convert the prefix to a mask, find the block size in the partial octet, and identify the block containing the given address. The block's first address is the network address; its last is the broadcast address. Addresses strictly between them are the ordinary host range. For 10.4.7.139/27, the block is .128 to .159, so hosts use .129 to .158.

## Work an address from start to finish

Take 172.16.5.214/28. A /28 has a block size of 16 in the last octet. The boundaries around 214 are 208 and 224, so the network is 172.16.5.208 and the next block begins at .224. The broadcast address is one less than that next boundary: 172.16.5.223. Ordinary host addresses run from .209 through .222.

This example gives another way to find the broadcast: take the next subnet's network address and subtract one. It reduces mistakes when listing a range. The network address is the first address of the block; the broadcast address is the last. Neither is assigned to an ordinary host in the conventional model.

For a /26, the block size is 64; for a /28, it is 16. Keep the prefix attached to the address throughout the calculation. An address without its prefix does not tell you which subnet boundaries to use.

assessmentSeed.prompt: What is the network address of 192.168.10.77/26?

lessons.title: The Seven Layers and Their Order
lessons.content:
# OSI Layer Architecture

## Seven layers, seven kinds of work

From top to bottom, the OSI model lists **Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical**. One memory aid is “All People Seem To Need Data Processing.” The model gives learners a shared vocabulary for discussing communication; it is not a claim that every real protocol fits neatly into one box.

The application layer supports services used by programs. Presentation concerns how information is represented. Session coordinates an exchange. Transport manages communication between endpoints. Network handles logical addressing and routing. Data Link moves frames across one local link. Physical carries bits as electrical, optical, or radio signals.

## Follow a request through the model

When a browser requests a page, the application creates data for the exchange. Lower layers prepare it for delivery, address it across networks, frame it for the current link, and transmit signals. The receiving system interprets the process in reverse. Each layer describes a responsibility, not necessarily a separate piece of hardware.

## Relate the model to familiar protocols

The seven OSI layers are a way to organise responsibilities, but Internet protocols are often described with a simpler four-layer TCP/IP model. The TCP/IP application layer broadly covers OSI's application, presentation, and session work; its transport layer aligns with OSI transport; Internet corresponds roughly to network; and link combines data-link and physical functions. The correspondence is approximate, not a perfect one-to-one mapping.

This distinction explains why a protocol may be placed differently in different textbooks. The OSI model is especially useful for learning and discussion because its layers separate tasks. Actual implementations combine functions and do not always follow the model's boundaries exactly.

When someone reports that “the network is down,” ask which function failed. Is there a signal? Can the device exchange local frames? Can it route to another network? Can the application reach its service? Layer names turn a broad complaint into specific questions that can be investigated.

assessmentSeed.prompt: Which OSI layer is responsible for logical addressing and routing?

lessons.title: Encapsulation, Addresses and Data Units
lessons.content:
# OSI Layer Architecture

## Headers carry instructions with the data

As information moves down the layers, each layer adds control information. This is **encapsulation**. A transport header can identify application ports; an IP header carries logical source and destination addresses; a data-link header supports delivery across the current local link. At the receiver, the matching layers read and remove their information, a process called **decapsulation**.

Names for protocol data units vary by layer and protocol: transport data is commonly called a TCP segment or UDP datagram, network-layer data a packet, and data-link data a frame. The physical layer transmits bits as signals.

## Keep the addresses distinct

An IP address helps a packet travel between networks. A link-layer address is used for the current local delivery. A port directs transport data to a service on a device. When a router forwards a packet onto another link, it normally builds a new link-layer frame for that next link; the IP destination remains the remote endpoint.

## A packet crosses more than one link

Suppose a laptop sends data to a server on another network. The transport data is placed inside an IP packet addressed to the server. To cross the laptop's local network, that packet is placed inside a frame addressed to the local router. The router removes the incoming frame, examines the IP destination, and forwards the packet inside a new frame for the next link.

The link-layer destination changes at each routed hop because each frame serves one local link. The packet's source and destination IP addresses usually remain end-to-end, except where a network function deliberately changes them. This is why an Ethernet address and an IP address answer different questions: one identifies a local delivery target; the other identifies the logical endpoint across networks.

Port numbers add another level of direction. A device may run several network services at once; the transport header helps deliver incoming data to the intended service. The layered headers work together rather than replacing one another.

assessmentSeed.prompt: At which OSI layer is an IP packet encapsulated inside a local-link frame?

lessons.title: Using OSI Layers to Troubleshoot
lessons.content:
# OSI Layer Architecture

## Troubleshoot from evidence

The OSI model is useful when a connection fails because it encourages a technician to separate possible causes. A disconnected cable or absent wireless signal points first to the Physical layer. If devices on the same local network cannot communicate, inspect link status and local addressing. If local communication works but remote networks do not, check the device's IP configuration, gateway, and routes.

A service can still fail after packets reach the device. A closed transport port, name-resolution problem, firewall rule, or application fault may all produce a similar browser message. A symptom alone does not identify a layer.

## Test one boundary at a time

Confirm the link, then test local communication, the default gateway, and finally the remote service. Record each result. A successful lower-layer test narrows the search but cannot prove that higher layers are working. For example, reaching a gateway shows local connectivity; it does not prove that a website is available or that its name resolves correctly.

## Use tests to narrow, not guess

Begin with observable facts. Check whether the network interface reports a link, then confirm the device has an address appropriate to its network. A self-assigned or unexpected address may point to a configuration or address-assignment issue. Next, test the default gateway. If that works, try a known remote IP address; if the address works but a name does not, investigate name resolution.

Each successful test narrows the likely fault, but it has limits. Reaching a remote IP does not prove that a particular website is running. Resolving a domain name does not prove that a firewall allows the service's traffic. A useful troubleshooting record includes the test, the result, and what the result rules in or out.

Avoid changing several settings at once. A controlled sequence makes cause and effect visible and lets another technician repeat the investigation. The OSI model provides categories for the evidence; it does not replace careful testing or knowledge of the actual network.

assessmentSeed.prompt: A disconnected network cable is primarily a fault at which OSI layer?

lessons.title: VLANs and Broadcast Domains
lessons.content:
# VLAN Configuration

## One switch, separate logical networks

A **virtual LAN (VLAN)** groups switch ports into a logical Layer 2 network. Devices attached to different ports can share a broadcast domain when their ports belong to the same VLAN. Two VLANs remain separate at Layer 2 even when they use the same physical switch. Traffic between them requires routing by a router or Layer 3 switch.

For example, an organisation might place staff computers and visitor devices in different VLANs. This controls which local broadcasts each group receives and makes policies easier to organise. Each VLAN normally has its own IP subnet and default gateway; a host placed in the wrong VLAN may receive an unexpected address or fail to reach its gateway.

## Separation is not encryption

A VLAN is useful network segmentation, but it does not encrypt data and should not be treated as a complete security boundary. Routing rules and access controls determine what traffic may cross between VLANs. The physical cable can be shared while the logical networks remain distinct.

## A VLAN needs a path to other networks

Devices in the same VLAN can exchange local traffic through switching. A device in one VLAN cannot reach a device in another VLAN by Layer 2 switching alone. A router or Layer 3 switch must receive the traffic, apply its routing decision, and send it into the destination VLAN. This is called inter-VLAN routing.

For example, a school might separate administrative computers, classroom devices, and visitors. Each VLAN can have its own subnet and gateway. A policy can permit classroom devices to reach a learning server while limiting access to administrative systems. The policy is enforced by routing and access controls, not by the VLAN number itself.

Broadcasts sent within one VLAN are not normally forwarded into another VLAN. This can reduce unnecessary local traffic, but it does not eliminate all network traffic or guarantee privacy. Proper addressing, routing, and access rules must be designed together for the separation to serve its purpose.

assessmentSeed.prompt: What separates the broadcast domains of two VLANs?

lessons.title: Access Ports, Trunks and VLAN Tags
lessons.content:
# VLAN Configuration

## Access ports meet end devices

An **access port** normally connects a computer, printer, or similar endpoint to one VLAN. The endpoint sends ordinary Ethernet frames; the switch associates them with the VLAN assigned to that port. The device does not need to choose or read a VLAN tag.

A **trunk** carries traffic for multiple VLANs between network devices. The IEEE 802.1Q standard inserts a tag into Ethernet frames so the receiving switch can identify the VLAN. Both ends must agree on trunk settings and on which VLANs are allowed to cross. A VLAN omitted from the allowed list cannot use that trunk, even if it exists on both switches.

## Follow one frame

A computer sends an untagged frame into its access port. The switch associates it with the port's VLAN and adds a tag when sending it across a trunk. The receiving switch reads the tag, removes it when forwarding toward an access port, and delivers the ordinary frame to the endpoint. Access and trunk ports solve different jobs and are not interchangeable.

## VLAN tags are local link information

An 802.1Q tag identifies a VLAN as a frame crosses a trunk. The tag is not an IP address and does not travel as an end-to-end identity through every router. When a router forwards the packet onto a new Ethernet link, it creates a frame appropriate to that link and its VLAN configuration.

An access port usually sends and receives untagged frames for one assigned VLAN. A trunk can carry several VLANs at once, but both switches must agree on trunk operation and allowed VLANs. Some networks also define how untagged frames on a trunk are treated; inconsistent settings can lead to confusing connectivity problems.

When diagnosing a host that cannot reach a peer in another switch area, trace the frame path: endpoint port, trunk, receiving switch, and destination port. Verify the VLAN at each boundary. A correct IP configuration cannot compensate for a VLAN being absent from the trunk that should carry its traffic.

assessmentSeed.prompt: Which standard adds VLAN identification to Ethernet frames on a trunk?

lessons.title: Planning and Verifying VLAN Membership
lessons.content:
# VLAN Configuration

## Plan membership before changing ports

For each VLAN, record its purpose, identifier, subnet, gateway, and the ports that need membership. Assign end-device ports to the intended VLAN. Configure switch-to-switch links as trunks and allow only the VLANs that need to cross them. Keep the treatment of untagged traffic consistent at both ends.

Verification should follow the same path as the traffic. Confirm that the VLAN exists, the endpoint port belongs to it, and every required trunk carries it. Then inspect the host's address, mask, and gateway. Test communication with another device in the same VLAN before testing a routed destination.

## Find the boundary where communication stops

If local devices in one VLAN work but a second VLAN is missing across a switch link, inspect trunk membership. If a host can reach peers in its own VLAN but not other subnets, investigate the Layer 3 gateway and its routing or access-control policy. Make one change at a time and verify it; changing several settings together hides which one mattered.

## Read symptoms against the network plan

Suppose two computers in VLAN 30 can communicate when connected to one switch, but a computer on another switch cannot reach them. The first computers show that local VLAN membership may be sound. The fault may lie in the inter-switch trunk: VLAN 30 could be missing from the allowed list, or the trunk may not be operating as expected. Check the planned path before changing the hosts' addresses.

If all devices in a VLAN have addresses but cannot reach their gateway, verify that the gateway interface exists for the correct subnet and that the switch ports and trunks carry the VLAN to it. If the gateway responds but another subnet does not, investigate routing and any access-control policy between networks.

Keep a record of the intended VLAN-to-subnet mapping. Comparing observed settings with a simple plan often reveals a mismatch faster than inspecting devices at random. After a correction, repeat the same test that originally failed.

assessmentSeed.prompt: Which setting should be checked when a VLAN works locally but is missing across a switch link?

lessons.title: Routes, Next Hops and Packet Forwarding
lessons.content:
# Routing Protocols

## A router chooses the next step

A router compares a packet's destination IP address with entries in its **routing table**. Each route describes a destination network and an outgoing interface or next hop. When more than one route matches, the router normally selects the most specific one: the route with the longest matching prefix.

If the destination is on a directly connected network, the router can send the packet on that link. Otherwise, it forwards the packet to the next router named by the selected route. That next hop is a neighbour, not necessarily the final destination. Each router along the path makes its own forwarding decision.

## What if no route matches?

Without a matching route, the router drops the packet unless a default route supplies a next step. A default route is less specific than ordinary network routes and is used only when no more specific entry applies. Longest-prefix matching lets a table contain both broad routes and precise exceptions without ambiguity.

## Longest prefix gives the closer match

Imagine a routing table with a route for 10.0.0.0/8 and a more specific route for 10.2.0.0/16. A packet for 10.2.5.8 matches both networks, but /16 matches more leading bits. The router therefore chooses the /16 route. A packet for 10.7.5.8 matches the /8 route but not the /16 route, so the broader entry applies.

This rule is called longest-prefix match. It is not the same as choosing the route with the fewest routers or the shortest physical distance. Once the matching route is selected, other routing information can determine which next hop is used for that destination.

The next hop should be reachable through an outgoing interface. If the route points to an invalid or unavailable neighbour, the packet may not progress even though a matching entry exists. Routing is a chain of local decisions: each router must have a usable route for the packet's destination.

assessmentSeed.prompt: When several routes match a destination, which one does a router prefer?
assessmentSeed.correct: The route with the longest matching prefix
distractors: The route with the shortest prefix
The route with the largest network address

lessons.title: Static Routes and Dynamic Routing
lessons.content:
# Routing Protocols

## Routes entered by hand

A **static route** is configured manually. It is predictable and can suit a small or stable network, but an administrator must update it when the topology changes. A default route may also be static; it provides a path for destinations not covered by a more specific entry.

## Routes learned from other routers

A **dynamic routing protocol** lets routers exchange reachability information and update routes as networks or links change. The protocol uses defined metrics and rules to compare possible paths. This can reduce manual work in a larger network, but it requires planning, monitoring, and a clear understanding of what routes are being shared.

Static and dynamic routes can coexist. An organisation might use a static route for a small branch and a dynamic protocol for its larger internal network. The best choice depends on network size, how often it changes, available expertise, and the consequences of a failed or outdated route; neither method is universally superior.

## Routes reflect a changing topology

In a small network with only a few fixed destinations, an administrator can enter static routes and document them. This keeps the routing table predictable. The trade-off appears when a link or destination changes: a static route does not automatically learn a new path, so someone must update it and verify the result.

Dynamic routing protocols exchange information so routers can learn which networks are reachable through neighbours. If a link fails, the protocol can recalculate or withdraw affected routes, subject to its convergence behaviour and configuration. This automation is useful at scale, but a mistaken advertisement or policy can spread incorrect information. Dynamic does not mean maintenance-free.

A default route is often used at a branch or endpoint network to send unknown destinations toward an upstream router. More specific routes still take precedence through longest-prefix matching. Administrators may combine a default route, carefully selected static routes, and a dynamic protocol where each fits the operational need.

assessmentSeed.prompt: What is a key feature of a static route?
assessmentSeed.correct: It is entered manually and does not automatically learn topology changes
distractors: It always chooses the physically shortest cable
It is learned from every neighbour automatically
It can only route within one VLAN

lessons.title: RIP, OSPF and BGP in Context
lessons.content:
# Routing Protocols

## Three protocols, different settings

**RIP** is a distance-vector protocol that uses hop count as its metric. Because its useful path length is limited to 15 hops, it is mainly suitable for small or teaching networks. **OSPF** is a link-state protocol commonly used within an organisation's autonomous system. Routers share information about links and calculate paths using a configured cost.

**BGP** exchanges reachability information between autonomous systems, the separately administered networks that make up the Internet. Its decisions can reflect policy and path attributes, not merely the number of routers crossed. BGP is therefore not simply a faster or larger version of RIP or OSPF.

## Choose by scope and purpose

RIP and OSPF are interior gateway protocols: they route within an organisation's routing domain. BGP is an exterior gateway protocol: it carries routing information between autonomous systems. The protocol choice follows the network's scale, policy, and operational needs. A short hop count alone does not guarantee the route an administrator wants.

## Metrics are not the whole routing decision

RIP's hop count is easy to understand: each router crossed adds a hop. That simplicity also limits how large a RIP-routed network can be. OSPF uses link-state information and a configured cost to calculate paths within an autonomous system. A low OSPF cost represents a preferred path according to the network's metric, not necessarily the shortest geographic route.

BGP works between autonomous systems and supports policy choices about which routes to accept and advertise. An Internet provider may prefer one route for business or operational reasons even if another path crosses fewer networks. Route selection therefore involves attributes and policy, not only physical distance.

The key question is the scope of the routing problem. Routing inside one organisation is generally handled by an interior gateway protocol such as OSPF; exchanging reachability between separately administered networks uses BGP. Knowing this distinction is more useful than trying to rank the protocols on one universal scale.

assessmentSeed.prompt: Which protocol is commonly used to exchange routes between autonomous systems?

lessons.title: Characteristics Used to Identify Living Things
lessons.content:
# Living & Non-Living Things

## Recognising life through linked processes

Living organisms carry out a group of life processes often remembered as MRS GREN: movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, and nutrition. Animals may move from place to place; a rooted plant moves parts and responds to light without walking. Movement alone is not a test for life.

Respiration is a chemical process in cells that releases usable energy from nutrients. It is not the same as breathing, which moves air into and out of lungs. Excretion removes waste products made by the organism; egestion removes undigested food from the digestive tract. Growth is a lasting increase in size or cell number, not simply a temporary swelling.

## Look beyond what is visible now

A dormant seed may show little activity, yet it is alive and can resume growth under suitable conditions. Classify an organism by the connected processes it can carry out over time, rather than expecting every process to be obvious at one moment.

## What the life processes mean

Nutrition is the taking in or making of materials needed for energy and growth. Animals obtain nutrients by eating; green plants make sugars using light, water, and carbon dioxide. Respiration releases usable energy from nutrients inside cells. Sensitivity is the ability to detect and respond to changes, such as a plant shoot growing toward light or a person pulling away from heat.

Reproduction produces new organisms of the same kind. It is a property of living systems, although an individual organism may be unable to reproduce at a particular stage of life. Excretion removes waste made by the body, such as carbon dioxide. It is different from egestion, which removes undigested food from the digestive system.

MRS GREN is a memory aid, not a set of isolated boxes. A living organism coordinates its processes: nutrition supplies materials, respiration releases energy, and growth uses materials to build new cells. Looking at this connected activity is more reliable than judging one visible movement.

assessmentSeed.prompt: Which process releases usable energy from food inside cells?

lessons.title: Comparing Living Things with Non-Living Things
lessons.content:
# Living & Non-Living Things

## One resemblance does not make life

Plants, animals, fungi, and microorganisms are living organisms. They are made of cells and carry out life processes. A stone does not feed, respire, or reproduce. Some non-living things imitate one feature of life, which is why classification needs more than a quick glance.

A flame spreads, uses fuel, and releases heat. A parked car can move when a person supplies energy. Neither example is an organism: a flame has no cells, and a car does not maintain itself through coordinated biological processes. A crystal can grow as material is added, but this is not growth through cell division and nutrition.

## Build a decision from evidence

Ask whether the object has cellular organisation and whether it carries out the life processes as a coordinated system. No single action—movement, growth, or energy use—is sufficient on its own. This approach explains why a dormant seed is alive while a spreading fire is not, despite the fire's dramatic movement and change.

## Compare living systems with imitations

A moving car has motion, but the motion comes from an engine and fuel supplied by people. The car does not grow by making new cells, remove its own metabolic waste, or reproduce cars through biological processes. A flame can spread and use fuel, but it has no cells or inherited biological organisation. Similarities in one feature do not make either one alive.

Some living things are easy to overlook. A seed may remain dormant until it has enough water, warmth, and oxygen. It does not move visibly during dormancy, but its cells remain capable of activity and growth. A fungus also may not travel from place to place; it obtains nutrients, grows, respires, and reproduces.

Classification is stronger when several kinds of evidence agree. Ask what the object is made of, where it obtains materials and energy, how it responds, and whether it can grow and reproduce as part of a living system. That reasoning handles edge cases better than a single yes-or-no test based on motion.

assessmentSeed.prompt: Why is a fire not classified as a living organism?
assessmentSeed.correct: It is not made of cells and does not carry out the coordinated life processes of an organism

lessons.title: Cells, Organisms and Their Environments
lessons.content:
# Living & Non-Living Things

## Cells form the living world

The **cell** is the basic unit of living structure and function. A unicellular organism, such as many bacteria, carries out all its life processes in one cell. A multicellular organism has many cells; some become specialised for particular work. Muscle cells contract, while red blood cells carry oxygen around the body.

In larger organisms, cells with related roles form tissues; tissues make organs, and organs work together in systems. Each level depends on the activity of cells. Organisms also exchange matter and energy with their surroundings. Green plants use light energy to make sugars from water and carbon dioxide; animals obtain nutrients by feeding.

## Organisms depend on their surroundings

Water, light, temperature, food, and shelter can affect growth and survival. A plant in a dark cupboard receives less light than one at a sunny window. Its response is not separate from the environment: living things interact with the conditions around them and with other organisms sharing the habitat.

## From cells to an organism's surroundings

In a multicellular animal, similar specialised cells can form a tissue, such as muscle tissue. Different tissues work together in an organ, such as the heart, and organs cooperate in systems that keep the organism alive. A single cell is not simply a smaller version of the whole body; it performs a particular role and depends on other cells for many conditions it needs.

A unicellular organism has no separate tissues or organs, but its one cell must still obtain materials, use energy, respond to conditions, and reproduce. This contrast shows that organisation can be simple or complex while the cell remains the basic unit of life.

An organism's environment includes non-living conditions such as temperature and water, as well as other organisms. A plant competes with nearby plants for light and water; an animal depends on food and shelter. Observing how a living thing responds to its surroundings helps explain why organisms are found in habitats that meet their needs.

assessmentSeed.prompt: What is the basic structural unit found in all living organisms?

lessons.title: Forms of Energy and Energy Transfer
lessons.content:
# Energy & Work

## Energy changes form and place

Energy is transferred between stores and can cause change. A moving ball has **kinetic energy**; an object raised above the ground has **gravitational potential energy**. Food and fuel store chemical energy. Thermal, electrical, light, and sound energy describe other familiar forms or transfer pathways.

When a ball falls, its gravitational potential energy decreases while its kinetic energy increases. In a torch, chemical energy in the battery is transferred electrically to the bulb, where energy becomes light and thermal energy. Some of the heating spreads to the surroundings rather than producing the useful light the user wants.

## Energy does not disappear

The law of conservation of energy says energy is not created or destroyed in a physical process; it is transferred or transformed. In everyday language, people may call energy “lost” when it becomes spread out and difficult to use. A careful account names the original store, the transfer, and where the energy ends up.

## Trace an energy transfer

An energy account should name where energy starts and where it goes. When a torch is switched on, chemical energy stored in the battery is transferred electrically through the circuit. The lamp transfers energy to light and thermal stores. The light is useful to the person reading; the heating is often an unwanted side effect, though it still represents energy transferred rather than destroyed.

When a ball is held above the ground, it has gravitational potential energy because of its position in Earth's gravitational field. As it falls, energy is transferred to its kinetic store. On impact, some energy transfers to sound, deformation, and heating. The ball may bounce, but each bounce is usually lower because energy spreads into the surroundings.

The term “energy loss” is common in everyday speech, but it means energy has left a useful store or pathway, not that the total energy has disappeared. Naming stores and transfers makes that distinction clear and helps compare devices fairly.

assessmentSeed.prompt: What happens to energy when a ball falls?
assessmentSeed.correct: Gravitational potential energy is transferred mainly into kinetic energy
distractors: The ball gains energy from nowhere

lessons.title: Work Done by a Force
lessons.content:
# Energy & Work

## A force does work when it moves an object

In physics, work is done when a force causes displacement. For a constant force acting in the direction of movement, **work done = force × distance**, or W = Fd. Work is measured in joules (J); one joule is one newton metre.

If a learner pushes a box with a 10 N force through 3 m in that direction, the work done on the box is 10 × 3 = 30 J. If the box does not move, its displacement is zero and the applied force does no mechanical work on it in this model, even though the learner may feel tired.

## Direction matters

Only the part of a force acting along the displacement contributes to work. A force at right angles to the movement does no work on the object in this calculation. When force and movement point in the same direction, multiply their magnitudes; include units so the result is clearly joules rather than newtons or metres.

## Include direction and units

Work is measured in joules. If a 15 N force moves a trolley 4 m in the same direction, W = Fd = 15 × 4 = 60 J. Write the units beside the values and the result; multiplying newtons by metres gives newton-metres, which are called joules.

When a force acts at an angle to the direction of movement, only its component along the movement does work. The more general relationship is W = Fd cos θ, where θ is the angle between the force and displacement. If the force is perpendicular to movement, cos 90° is zero, so that force does no work on the object in this model.

This explains why a person carrying a bag at constant height does no mechanical work on the bag in the direction of horizontal walking, even though the person uses energy internally. The physics definition focuses on the force component and the object's displacement, not on how tiring an activity feels.

assessmentSeed.prompt: A 10 N force moves a box 3 m in the same direction. How much work is done?

lessons.title: Power, Efficiency and Everyday Energy Use
lessons.content:
# Energy & Work

## Power measures the rate of transfer

Power tells us how quickly work is done or energy is transferred: **power = work ÷ time**, or P = W/t. It is measured in watts (W), and one watt equals one joule per second. Two motors may transfer the same energy, but the one that does it in less time has greater power.

A motor that transfers 600 J in 10 s has a power of 600 ÷ 10 = 60 W. Power is a rate, not the total energy used. If the motor runs longer, it transfers more energy even if its power stays the same.

## Efficiency compares useful output with input

Efficiency = useful energy output ÷ total energy input × 100%. If a pump receives 900 J and transfers 600 J usefully, its efficiency is about 66.7%. The remaining energy has not vanished; some spreads into less useful forms, often heating the motor and surroundings. In ordinary devices, useful output cannot exceed the total input.

## Compare devices with the same input

Suppose two lamps each receive 100 J of electrical energy. One transfers 20 J into useful light; the other transfers 35 J into useful light. Their efficiencies are 20% and 35%. The more efficient lamp provides more useful light for the same input, while the remaining energy in each case is transferred mostly to heating the surroundings.

Power and efficiency answer different questions. A high-power device transfers energy quickly; a high-efficiency device converts a larger share of its input into the output wanted. A powerful motor can still be inefficient, and a low-power device can still use its input efficiently.

Check calculations by estimating whether the answer makes sense. If useful output is larger than input, either the quantities have been mixed up or the system boundary is incomplete. If work is given in joules and time in seconds, dividing gives watts. Keep the units visible until the final step.

assessmentSeed.prompt: A device transfers 600 J in 10 s. What is its power?

lessons.title: Physical Changes and Chemical Reactions
lessons.content:
# Chemical Changes

## Ask whether a new substance formed

A **physical change** alters a substance's form or state without changing its chemical identity. When ice melts, solid water becomes liquid water; the molecules are still H2O. A **chemical reaction** forms one or more substances with different properties. Iron reacting with oxygen and water forms rust, which is not simply iron in a new shape.

Bubbles, a lasting colour change, a precipitate, or a temperature change may be evidence of a reaction. None proves it alone. Boiling water makes bubbles, for example, but the bubbles are water vapour and no new substance has formed. Look at the starting and final materials and ask what particles are present.

## Reversibility is only a clue

Many physical changes are easy to reverse, but reversibility is not the definition. A change is classified by whether the substance's chemical identity changes. Melting and freezing water are physical changes; burning magnesium in oxygen is chemical because magnesium oxide is produced.

## Sort changes by the substances present

Cutting paper changes its size and shape, but the paper remains paper. Dissolving sugar in water also does not by itself create a new substance; the sugar can be recovered by evaporating the water. These are physical changes. Burning paper is different: smoke, gases, and ash form, each with properties unlike the original paper.

Some reactions are difficult to reverse, but difficulty is not the test. A reaction is chemical when the particles rearrange to form different substances. A physical change can be hard to reverse in practice, while some chemical reactions can be reversed under suitable conditions.

Use observations as clues, not shortcuts. A colour change may result from mixing two coloured liquids without a reaction; bubbles may come from boiling. Ask what the starting materials were and what substances remain afterward. This question ties visible evidence to the definition instead of treating any dramatic change as proof of chemistry.

assessmentSeed.prompt: Which change forms a new substance?
assessmentSeed.correct: Iron reacting with oxygen to form rust

lessons.title: Reactants, Products and Word Equations
lessons.content:
# Chemical Changes

## Read a reaction from left to right

The substances present at the start of a reaction are **reactants**; those formed are **products**. A word equation places the reactants on the left and products on the right. For example: **magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide**. Read the arrow as “reacts to form.” It does not mean the atoms disappear.

In a reaction, atoms are rearranged as bonds break and new bonds form. The atoms of each element are conserved, even though they are grouped into different substances. This is why a correctly balanced chemical equation has the same number of each kind of atom on both sides.

## Separate observations from explanations

When magnesium burns, a bright light is something an observer sees; magnesium oxide is the product. Naming reactants and products explains what changed, while observations provide evidence. A gas or colour change may suggest a reaction, but compare the materials before and after to decide what actually formed.

## Word equations describe, but do not balance, atoms

Consider the word equation **carbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide**. Carbon and oxygen are the reactants; carbon dioxide is the product. The equation summarises the change in names, but it does not show how many atoms or molecules take part. A symbol equation adds that information and must be balanced so each element has the same number of atoms on both sides.

For magnesium reacting with oxygen, the word equation is **magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide**. Oxygen is present as molecules containing two oxygen atoms, so the symbol equation is 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO. There are two magnesium atoms and two oxygen atoms on each side. The coefficients show the relative numbers of particles; they do not change the identity of a formula.

At this level, practise naming reactants and products before balancing symbols. Reading from left to right helps distinguish what was present at the start from what the reaction produced.

assessmentSeed.prompt: In 'magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide', what is the product?

lessons.title: Conservation of Mass and Reaction Evidence
lessons.content:
# Chemical Changes

## Account for every atom

During a chemical reaction, atoms are rearranged into new substances. In a closed system, total mass stays constant: the mass of the reactants equals the mass of the products. Matter has not been created or destroyed; it has changed arrangement.

An open container can give a misleading measurement. Vinegar reacting with a carbonate can produce carbon dioxide gas. If the gas escapes, the balance no longer measures it, so the measured contents seem to lose mass. The gas is still matter; it has simply crossed the boundary of the measured system.

## Define the system before weighing

To test conservation fairly, include all products in the measurement. A sealed setup can trap the gas so it remains on the balance with the other products. When observations appear to contradict conservation, check whether a gas, liquid, or solid entered or left the system. The boundary of the experiment matters as much as the reading on the scale.

## Design a fair mass measurement

To test conservation of mass in a gas-producing reaction, weigh the complete setup before and after the reaction. A sealed flask with a stopper can keep carbon dioxide from escaping, provided the setup is designed safely and the gas has space to form. The mass of the flask, reactants, and products is included both times, so the readings should be the same within the balance's precision.

If the reaction is measured in an open cup, some gas enters the surrounding air. The balance then measures less material, even though the total matter has not changed. The error is not in the conservation principle; the measured system excluded part of the products after they escaped.

Every experiment has a boundary: decide what is inside the system and what the balance includes. Record the initial and final setup consistently. If a result differs slightly, consider measurement limits, spills, evaporation, or gas escaping before concluding that mass was destroyed.

assessmentSeed.prompt: Why can an open container appear to lose mass during a gas-producing reaction?
assessmentSeed.correct: Some product gas escapes and is no longer on the balance

lessons.title: The Sun, Planets and Smaller Solar-System Bodies
lessons.content:
# Solar System

## A star and the objects bound to it

The Solar System consists of the Sun and the objects held in orbit around it by gravity. The Sun is a star. In order from the Sun, the eight planets are **Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus,** and **Neptune**. The first four are rocky inner planets. Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants; Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.

The system also includes moons, dwarf planets, asteroids, comets, and smaller pieces of rock and dust. A moon orbits a planet. Asteroids and comets orbit the Sun. A dwarf planet also orbits the Sun, but it has not cleared other objects from its orbital neighbourhood; Pluto is one example.

## Gravity and reflected light

The Sun's gravity continually changes a planet's direction while the planet moves forward, producing an orbit. Planets do not make their own visible light; we see them because they reflect sunlight. These different bodies belong to one system, but their sizes, compositions, and paths vary widely.

## Compare the inner and outer planets

Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars are relatively small, rocky planets with solid surfaces. Beyond Mars lies the asteroid belt, followed by the giant planets. Jupiter and Saturn are called gas giants because they consist mainly of hydrogen and helium. Uranus and Neptune contain larger proportions of substances such as water, ammonia, and methane in deep, cold layers, so they are often called ice giants.

The names describe broad composition, not a claim that every planet has a simple solid surface like Earth's. The giant planets have rings and many moons; the rocky planets also have moons, except Mercury and Venus. Their differences reflect how materials were distributed in the early Solar System and how each planet developed.

The Sun contains most of the Solar System's mass, and its gravity governs the planets' orbits. Smaller bodies also orbit the Sun, while moons orbit planets. Keeping track of what each object orbits is a useful way to distinguish a moon from a planet or asteroid.

assessmentSeed.prompt: Which planet is third from the Sun?

lessons.title: Rotation, Revolution, Day and Year
lessons.content:
# Solar System

## Spinning and travelling around another body

**Rotation** is the spin of a body on its axis. Earth completes a rotation in about 24 hours. As it spins, locations turn toward the Sun and then away, producing the cycle of day and night. **Revolution** is movement around another body. Earth takes about one year to complete one revolution around the Sun.

These motions describe different things: rotation sets the length of a day, while revolution sets the length of a year. A place facing the Sun has daylight; the opposite side of Earth is in darkness. The boundary between them moves as Earth rotates.

## The Moon also moves

The Moon revolves around Earth and rotates on its axis. Its rotation and orbital periods are nearly the same, so the same general side faces Earth over time. Its phases do not result from Earth's daily rotation or from Earth's shadow; they arise as the Moon's position changes and we see different portions of its sunlit half.

## Why the Sun appears to cross the sky

The Sun's apparent movement from east to west during the day is mainly a result of Earth's rotation from west to east. Earth turns once in about 24 hours, so a location rotates into sunlight, passes through daylight, and later rotates into darkness. The Sun does not need to travel around Earth for this daily pattern to occur.

Earth's revolution takes about 365 and a quarter days. The calendar accounts for the extra quarter day by adding a leap day in most years divisible by four, with century-year exceptions. This adjustment keeps the calendar aligned with Earth's orbit over time.

Rotation and revolution should not be confused with the Moon's phases. The Moon's changing position around Earth changes how much of its sunlit half we can see. During an ordinary phase, Earth is not casting a shadow on the Moon. The shadow explanation applies to a lunar eclipse, which occurs only when the bodies align appropriately.

assessmentSeed.prompt: Which motion of Earth produces the day-and-night cycle?

lessons.title: Earth's Tilt, Seasons and the Moon's Phases
lessons.content:
# Solar System

## Tilt changes the sunlight each hemisphere receives

Earth's axis is tilted by about 23.5 degrees relative to the plane of its orbit. As Earth travels around the Sun, each hemisphere takes a turn tilted toward it and then away. A hemisphere tilted toward the Sun receives more direct sunlight and has longer days; tilted away, it receives less direct sunlight and has shorter days. These changes produce the seasons. The two hemispheres experience opposite seasons at the same time.

Earth's changing distance from the Sun is not the main cause of the seasons. The axial tilt changes both the angle and duration of sunlight over the year.

## The Moon's phases are a matter of viewpoint

The Sun illuminates half of the Moon at all times. As the Moon orbits Earth, we see different portions of that lit half, from crescent to quarter to full and back. At new moon, the lit side faces mostly away from us; at full moon, we see nearly all of it. A lunar eclipse is different: Earth moves between the Sun and Moon and its shadow falls on the Moon.

## Follow the Moon through a month

The Moon's phases follow a repeating cycle. After new moon, the visible lit portion grows: it is waxing. Around first quarter, we see half of the visible face illuminated. At full moon, the near side appears fully lit. The illuminated portion then shrinks, or wanes, passing through last quarter before returning to new moon. The exact appearance depends on the Moon's position relative to Earth and the Sun.

A lunar eclipse is not the same as a monthly phase. It happens when Earth lies between the Sun and Moon and its shadow reaches the Moon. A solar eclipse has a different alignment: the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun and blocks some sunlight for observers in a limited area. Eclipses do not happen every month because the Moon's orbit is tilted relative to Earth's orbit around the Sun.

Seasonal sunlight follows Earth's axial tilt, not the Moon's phases. Keeping these patterns separate helps explain why seasons change over a year while lunar phases repeat roughly each month.

assessmentSeed.prompt: What is the main cause of Earth's seasons?
assessmentSeed.correct: Earth's tilted axis as it orbits the Sun
distractors: Earth's changing distance from the Moon
